case_info.scenario: A 52-year-old woman presented with decreased vision in both eyes. She was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 3 months before presentation, with a hemoglobin A1cof 13%. At that time, she was given metformin and semaglutide for glucose control. Her visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/200 OS. Fundus examination revealed retinal hemorrhages, hard exudates, and microaneurysms bilaterally (Figure, A and B). Fluorescein angiography revealed microaneurysms with noncentral leakage in the posterior pole with absence of significant ischemia and capillary dropout. Optical coherence tomography scans from the same day showed retinal edema with intraretinal fluid accumulation in both eyes (central subfield thickness: 320 nm OD, 764 nm OS) with foveal detachment in the left eye. She was diagnosed with severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy with macular edema in both eyes. She received 2 and 3 injections of bevacizumab in the right and left eyes, respectively, followed by 2 injections of aflibercept in both eyes with minimal effect on the edema. Blood analysis showed the following values: hemoglobin, 10.4 g/dL; red blood cell count, 3.30 × 106/μL; white blood cell count, 10 470/μL; platelets, 197 × 103/μL; fasting blood glucose, 150 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0555); normal lipid profile; and creatinine, 1.2 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4). Hemoglobin A1cdecreased to 6.8% at 7 months after presentation.
case_info.caption: Widefield late-phase fluorescence angiography images of the right (A) and left (B) eye demonstrating areas of microaneurysms with mild leakage and absence of serious ischemia or capillary dropout. The top left insert in each panel shows the pseudocolor widefield fundus photographs demonstrating retinal hemorrhages, hard exudates, and microaneurysms in the right and left eye. The bottom inserts of each panel show macular optical coherence tomography imaging at presentation (bottom left) and after the patient received intravitreal injections (bottom right) over 6 months. The right eye demonstrates refractory retinal edema. The left eye demonstrates refractory retinal edema with neuroretinal detachment. The white asterisks indicate intraretinal edema; the yellow asterisks indicates neuroretinal detachment.
case_info.explanation: Immunoglobulin (Ig) A multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy A. Order serum protein electrophoresis The lack of substantial central macular leakage on fluorescein angiography suggests that abnormal vascular permeability was not the major mechanism for the edema, and thus, injection of additional or alternative anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (C) or intravitreal corticosteroids (B) would likely not have helped. Although semaglutide (D) has been associated with worsening diabetic retinopathy, the patient had macular edema shortly after starting semaglutide, making it unlikely to be the cause of the macular edema. Additionally, worsening diabetic retinopathy associated with glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists is not commonly associated with worsening macular edema. Although the shape of the foveal detachment in the left eye is unusual for diabetic macular edema, this alone would not warrant workup for a nondiabetic cause of the retinal findings. However, in conjunction with the lack of response to anti-VEGF injections and atypical fluorescein angiography findings, further workup for a nondiabetic cause of the findings is indicated. Baseline laboratory work revealed anemia, elevated white blood cell count, and elevated serum creatinine, raising suspicion for a hyperviscosity syndrome. Thus, serum protein electrophoresis (A) was recommended as the next step in the workup. This step revealed an M-spike, which prompted quantitative immunoglobin analysis that revealed an elevated IgA result (2441 mg/dL). Bone marrow biopsy revealed 40% to 50% plasma cell infiltration, confirming the diagnosis of IgA multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy. Paraproteinemia describes the presence of excessive monoclonal globulins in the blood, typically due to underlying immunoproliferative disorders such as Waldenström macroglobulinemia or multiple myeloma.1Excessive paraprotein in the blood leads to hyperviscosity, which can manifest as venous stasis retinopathy, retinal hemorrhages, and optic disc edema. An infrequent issue in paraproteinemic maculopathy is the presence of serous macular detachment.1-5It is proposed that hyperviscosity causes venous stasis and hypoxia of the endothelial cells, weakening the blood-retinal barrier, leading to accumulation of immunoglobulins in the subretinal space. The consequent osmotic gradient created by the immunoglobulins leads to serous macular detachments.1,5-7Additionally, risk factors like anemia and diabetes can exacerbate the process by inducing hypoxia and further damaging the blood-retinal barrier, leading to increased leakage of immunoglobulins.1 Primary treatment is directed at decreasing blood paraprotein levels through systemic treatments.8In a case series of 33 patients with paraproteinemic maculopathy, there was no definitive improvement with intravitreal anti-VEGF or corticosteroid agents. The long-term visual prognosis is guarded, with approximately 40% of cases having unchanged or worsening maculopathy despite adequate treatment of paraproteinemia.1 Patients with type 2 diabetes frequently have subclinical diabetes years before being diagnosed. Patients can present with advanced retinopathy shortly after diagnosis, thus making it an important differential to consider. However, this case underscores the importance of considering hyperviscosity syndromes for patients with diabetes and atypical macular edema unresponsive to anti-VEGF treatment. Early diagnosis is crucial because ocular symptoms may be the first indicators of paraproteinemia. The patient was referred to an oncologist and began chemotherapy. Twelve weeks later, her visual acuity improved to 20/40 OD and 20/80 OS. On optical coherence tomography, the central subfield thicknesses changed to 435 nm OD and 406 nm OS. Her IgA level improved to 106 mg/dL.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Optical coherence tomography scans from the same day showed retinal edema with intraretinal fluid accumulation in both eyes (central subfield thickness: 320 nm OD, 764 nm OS) with foveal detachment in the left eye. She was diagnosed with severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy with macular edema in both eyes. She received 2 and 3 injections of bevacizumab in the right and left eyes, respectively, followed by 2 injections of aflibercept in both eyes with minimal effect on the edema. case_info.explanation: Immunoglobulin (Ig) A multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy A. Order serum protein electrophoresis The lack of substantial central macular leakage on fluorescein angiography suggests that abnormal vascular permeability was not the major mechanism for the edema, and thus, injection of additional or alternative anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (C) or intravitreal corticosteroids (B) would likely not have helped. Although semaglutide (D) has been associated with worsening diabetic retinopathy, the patient had macular edema shortly after starting semaglutide, making it unlikely to be the cause of the macular edema. Additionally, worsening diabetic retinopathy associated with glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists is not commonly associated with worsening macular edema. Although the shape of the foveal detachment in the left eye is unusual for diabetic macular edema, this alone would not warrant workup for a nondiabetic cause of the retinal findings. However, in conjunction with the lack of response to anti-VEGF injections and atypical fluorescein angiography findings, further workup for a nondiabetic cause of the findings is indicated. Baseline laboratory work revealed anemia, elevated white blood cell count, and elevated serum creatinine, raising suspicion for a hyperviscosity syndrome. Thus, serum protein electrophoresis (A) was recommended as the next step in the workup. This step revealed an M-spike, which prompted quantitative immunoglobin analysis that revealed an elevated IgA result (2441 mg/dL). Bone marrow biopsy revealed 40% to 50% plasma cell infiltration, confirming the diagnosis of IgA multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy. Paraproteinemia describes the presence of excessive monoclonal globulins in the blood, typically due to underlying immunoproliferative disorders such as Waldenström macroglobulinemia or multiple myeloma.1Excessive paraprotein in the blood leads to hyperviscosity, which can manifest as venous stasis retinopathy, retinal hemorrhages, and optic disc edema. An infrequent issue in paraproteinemic maculopathy is the presence of serous macular detachment.1-5It is proposed that hyperviscosity causes venous stasis and hypoxia of the endothelial cells, weakening the blood-retinal barrier, leading to accumulation of immunoglobulins in the subretinal space. The consequent osmotic gradient created by the immunoglobulins leads to serous macular detachments.1,5-7Additionally, risk factors like anemia and diabetes can exacerbate the process by inducing hypoxia and further damaging the blood-retinal barrier, leading to increased leakage of immunoglobulins.1 Primary treatment is directed at decreasing blood paraprotein levels through systemic treatments.8In a case series of 33 patients with paraproteinemic maculopathy, there was no definitive improvement with intravitreal anti-VEGF or corticosteroid agents. The long-term visual prognosis is guarded, with approximately 40% of cases having unchanged or worsening maculopathy despite adequate treatment of paraproteinemia.1 Patients with type 2 diabetes frequently have subclinical diabetes years before being diagnosed. Patients can present with advanced retinopathy shortly after diagnosis, thus making it an important differential to consider. However, this case underscores the importance of considering hyperviscosity syndromes for patients with diabetes and atypical macular edema unresponsive to anti-VEGF treatment. Early diagnosis is crucial because ocular symptoms may be the first indicators of paraproteinemia. The patient was referred to an oncologist and began chemotherapy. Twelve weeks later, her visual acuity improved to 20/40 OD and 20/80 OS. On optical coherence tomography, the central subfield thicknesses changed to 435 nm OD and 406 nm OS. Her IgA level improved to 106 mg/dL.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

case_info.explanation: Immunoglobulin (Ig) A multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy A. Order serum protein electrophoresis The lack of substantial central macular leakage on fluorescein angiography suggests that abnormal vascular permeability was not the major mechanism for the edema, and thus, injection of additional or alternative anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (C) or intravitreal corticosteroids (B) would likely not have helped. Although semaglutide (D) has been associated with worsening diabetic retinopathy, the patient had macular edema shortly after starting semaglutide, making it unlikely to be the cause of the macular edema. Additionally, worsening diabetic retinopathy associated with glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists is not commonly associated with worsening macular edema. Although the shape of the foveal detachment in the left eye is unusual for diabetic macular edema, this alone would not warrant workup for a nondiabetic cause of the retinal findings. However, in conjunction with the lack of response to anti-VEGF injections and atypical fluorescein angiography findings, further workup for a nondiabetic cause of the findings is indicated. Baseline laboratory work revealed anemia, elevated white blood cell count, and elevated serum creatinine, raising suspicion for a hyperviscosity syndrome. Thus, serum protein electrophoresis (A) was recommended as the next step in the workup. This step revealed an M-spike, which prompted quantitative immunoglobin analysis that revealed an elevated IgA result (2441 mg/dL). Bone marrow biopsy revealed 40% to 50% plasma cell infiltration, confirming the diagnosis of IgA multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy. Paraproteinemia describes the presence of excessive monoclonal globulins in the blood, typically due to underlying immunoproliferative disorders such as Waldenström macroglobulinemia or multiple myeloma.1Excessive paraprotein in the blood leads to hyperviscosity, which can manifest as venous stasis retinopathy, retinal hemorrhages, and optic disc edema. An infrequent issue in paraproteinemic maculopathy is the presence of serous macular detachment.1-5It is proposed that hyperviscosity causes venous stasis and hypoxia of the endothelial cells, weakening the blood-retinal barrier, leading to accumulation of immunoglobulins in the subretinal space. The consequent osmotic gradient created by the immunoglobulins leads to serous macular detachments.1,5-7Additionally, risk factors like anemia and diabetes can exacerbate the process by inducing hypoxia and further damaging the blood-retinal barrier, leading to increased leakage of immunoglobulins.1 Primary treatment is directed at decreasing blood paraprotein levels through systemic treatments.8In a case series of 33 patients with paraproteinemic maculopathy, there was no definitive improvement with intravitreal anti-VEGF or corticosteroid agents. The long-term visual prognosis is guarded, with approximately 40% of cases having unchanged or worsening maculopathy despite adequate treatment of paraproteinemia.1 Patients with type 2 diabetes frequently have subclinical diabetes years before being diagnosed. Patients can present with advanced retinopathy shortly after diagnosis, thus making it an important differential to consider. However, this case underscores the importance of considering hyperviscosity syndromes for patients with diabetes and atypical macular edema unresponsive to anti-VEGF treatment. Early diagnosis is crucial because ocular symptoms may be the first indicators of paraproteinemia. The patient was referred to an oncologist and began chemotherapy. Twelve weeks later, her visual acuity improved to 20/40 OD and 20/80 OS. On optical coherence tomography, the central subfield thicknesses changed to 435 nm OD and 406 nm OS. Her IgA level improved to 106 mg/dL.

2. Performance

3. Effort

       competing options already qualifies.

4. Frustration

   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.explanation: Immunoglobulin (Ig) A multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy A. Order serum protein electrophoresis The lack of substantial central macular leakage on fluorescein angiography suggests that abnormal vascular permeability was not the major mechanism for the edema, and thus, injection of additional or alternative anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (C) or intravitreal corticosteroids (B) would likely not have helped. Although semaglutide (D) has been associated with worsening diabetic retinopathy, the patient had macular edema shortly after starting semaglutide, making it unlikely to be the cause of the macular edema. Additionally, worsening diabetic retinopathy associated with glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists is not commonly associated with worsening macular edema. Although the shape of the foveal detachment in the left eye is unusual for diabetic macular edema, this alone would not warrant workup for a nondiabetic cause of the retinal findings. However, in conjunction with the lack of response to anti-VEGF injections and atypical fluorescein angiography findings, further workup for a nondiabetic cause of the findings is indicated. Baseline laboratory work revealed anemia, elevated white blood cell count, and elevated serum creatinine, raising suspicion for a hyperviscosity syndrome. Thus, serum protein electrophoresis (A) was recommended as the next step in the workup. This step revealed an M-spike, which prompted quantitative immunoglobin analysis that revealed an elevated IgA result (2441 mg/dL). Bone marrow biopsy revealed 40% to 50% plasma cell infiltration, confirming the diagnosis of IgA multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy. Paraproteinemia describes the presence of excessive monoclonal globulins in the blood, typically due to underlying immunoproliferative disorders such as Waldenström macroglobulinemia or multiple myeloma.1Excessive paraprotein in the blood leads to hyperviscosity, which can manifest as venous stasis retinopathy, retinal hemorrhages, and optic disc edema. An infrequent issue in paraproteinemic maculopathy is the presence of serous macular detachment.1-5It is proposed that hyperviscosity causes venous stasis and hypoxia of the endothelial cells, weakening the blood-retinal barrier, leading to accumulation of immunoglobulins in the subretinal space. The consequent osmotic gradient created by the immunoglobulins leads to serous macular detachments.1,5-7Additionally, risk factors like anemia and diabetes can exacerbate the process by inducing hypoxia and further damaging the blood-retinal barrier, leading to increased leakage of immunoglobulins.1 Primary treatment is directed at decreasing blood paraprotein levels through systemic treatments.8In a case series of 33 patients with paraproteinemic maculopathy, there was no definitive improvement with intravitreal anti-VEGF or corticosteroid agents. The long-term visual prognosis is guarded, with approximately 40% of cases having unchanged or worsening maculopathy despite adequate treatment of paraproteinemia.1 Patients with type 2 diabetes frequently have subclinical diabetes years before being diagnosed. Patients can present with advanced retinopathy shortly after diagnosis, thus making it an important differential to consider. However, this case underscores the importance of considering hyperviscosity syndromes for patients with diabetes and atypical macular edema unresponsive to anti-VEGF treatment. Early diagnosis is crucial because ocular symptoms may be the first indicators of paraproteinemia. The patient was referred to an oncologist and began chemotherapy. Twelve weeks later, her visual acuity improved to 20/40 OD and 20/80 OS. On optical coherence tomography, the central subfield thicknesses changed to 435 nm OD and 406 nm OS. Her IgA level improved to 106 mg/dL.

   Definition:

   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:

     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: Immunoglobulin (Ig) A multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy A. Order serum protein electrophoresis The lack of substantial central macular leakage on fluorescein angiography suggests that abnormal vascular permeability was not the major mechanism for the edema, and thus, injection of additional or alternative anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (C) or intravitreal corticosteroids (B) would likely not have helped. Although semaglutide (D) has been associated with worsening diabetic retinopathy, the patient had macular edema shortly after starting semaglutide, making it unlikely to be the cause of the macular edema. Additionally, worsening diabetic retinopathy associated with glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists is not commonly associated with worsening macular edema. Although the shape of the foveal detachment in the left eye is unusual for diabetic macular edema, this alone would not warrant workup for a nondiabetic cause of the retinal findings. However, in conjunction with the lack of response to anti-VEGF injections and atypical fluorescein angiography findings, further workup for a nondiabetic cause of the findings is indicated. Baseline laboratory work revealed anemia, elevated white blood cell count, and elevated serum creatinine, raising suspicion for a hyperviscosity syndrome. Thus, serum protein electrophoresis (A) was recommended as the next step in the workup. This step revealed an M-spike, which prompted quantitative immunoglobin analysis that revealed an elevated IgA result (2441 mg/dL). Bone marrow biopsy revealed 40% to 50% plasma cell infiltration, confirming the diagnosis of IgA multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy. Paraproteinemia describes the presence of excessive monoclonal globulins in the blood, typically due to underlying immunoproliferative disorders such as Waldenström macroglobulinemia or multiple myeloma.1Excessive paraprotein in the blood leads to hyperviscosity, which can manifest as venous stasis retinopathy, retinal hemorrhages, and optic disc edema. An infrequent issue in paraproteinemic maculopathy is the presence of serous macular detachment.1-5It is proposed that hyperviscosity causes venous stasis and hypoxia of the endothelial cells, weakening the blood-retinal barrier, leading to accumulation of immunoglobulins in the subretinal space. The consequent osmotic gradient created by the immunoglobulins leads to serous macular detachments.1,5-7Additionally, risk factors like anemia and diabetes can exacerbate the process by inducing hypoxia and further damaging the blood-retinal barrier, leading to increased leakage of immunoglobulins.1 Primary treatment is directed at decreasing blood paraprotein levels through systemic treatments.8In a case series of 33 patients with paraproteinemic maculopathy, there was no definitive improvement with intravitreal anti-VEGF or corticosteroid agents. The long-term visual prognosis is guarded, with approximately 40% of cases having unchanged or worsening maculopathy despite adequate treatment of paraproteinemia.1 Patients with type 2 diabetes frequently have subclinical diabetes years before being diagnosed. Patients can present with advanced retinopathy shortly after diagnosis, thus making it an important differential to consider. However, this case underscores the importance of considering hyperviscosity syndromes for patients with diabetes and atypical macular edema unresponsive to anti-VEGF treatment. Early diagnosis is crucial because ocular symptoms may be the first indicators of paraproteinemia. The patient was referred to an oncologist and began chemotherapy. Twelve weeks later, her visual acuity improved to 20/40 OD and 20/80 OS. On optical coherence tomography, the central subfield thicknesses changed to 435 nm OD and 406 nm OS. Her IgA level improved to 106 mg/dL.

case_info.explanation: Immunoglobulin (Ig) A multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy A. Order serum protein electrophoresis The lack of substantial central macular leakage on fluorescein angiography suggests that abnormal vascular permeability was not the major mechanism for the edema, and thus, injection of additional or alternative anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (C) or intravitreal corticosteroids (B) would likely not have helped. Although semaglutide (D) has been associated with worsening diabetic retinopathy, the patient had macular edema shortly after starting semaglutide, making it unlikely to be the cause of the macular edema. Additionally, worsening diabetic retinopathy associated with glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists is not commonly associated with worsening macular edema. Although the shape of the foveal detachment in the left eye is unusual for diabetic macular edema, this alone would not warrant workup for a nondiabetic cause of the retinal findings. However, in conjunction with the lack of response to anti-VEGF injections and atypical fluorescein angiography findings, further workup for a nondiabetic cause of the findings is indicated. Baseline laboratory work revealed anemia, elevated white blood cell count, and elevated serum creatinine, raising suspicion for a hyperviscosity syndrome. Thus, serum protein electrophoresis (A) was recommended as the next step in the workup. This step revealed an M-spike, which prompted quantitative immunoglobin analysis that revealed an elevated IgA result (2441 mg/dL). Bone marrow biopsy revealed 40% to 50% plasma cell infiltration, confirming the diagnosis of IgA multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy. Paraproteinemia describes the presence of excessive monoclonal globulins in the blood, typically due to underlying immunoproliferative disorders such as Waldenström macroglobulinemia or multiple myeloma.1Excessive paraprotein in the blood leads to hyperviscosity, which can manifest as venous stasis retinopathy, retinal hemorrhages, and optic disc edema. An infrequent issue in paraproteinemic maculopathy is the presence of serous macular detachment.1-5It is proposed that hyperviscosity causes venous stasis and hypoxia of the endothelial cells, weakening the blood-retinal barrier, leading to accumulation of immunoglobulins in the subretinal space. The consequent osmotic gradient created by the immunoglobulins leads to serous macular detachments.1,5-7Additionally, risk factors like anemia and diabetes can exacerbate the process by inducing hypoxia and further damaging the blood-retinal barrier, leading to increased leakage of immunoglobulins.1 Primary treatment is directed at decreasing blood paraprotein levels through systemic treatments.8In a case series of 33 patients with paraproteinemic maculopathy, there was no definitive improvement with intravitreal anti-VEGF or corticosteroid agents. The long-term visual prognosis is guarded, with approximately 40% of cases having unchanged or worsening maculopathy despite adequate treatment of paraproteinemia.1 Patients with type 2 diabetes frequently have subclinical diabetes years before being diagnosed. Patients can present with advanced retinopathy shortly after diagnosis, thus making it an important differential to consider. However, this case underscores the importance of considering hyperviscosity syndromes for patients with diabetes and atypical macular edema unresponsive to anti-VEGF treatment. Early diagnosis is crucial because ocular symptoms may be the first indicators of paraproteinemia. The patient was referred to an oncologist and began chemotherapy. Twelve weeks later, her visual acuity improved to 20/40 OD and 20/80 OS. On optical coherence tomography, the central subfield thicknesses changed to 435 nm OD and 406 nm OS. Her IgA level improved to 106 mg/dL.

[Case]
A 52-year-old woman presented with decreased vision in both eyes. She was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 3 months before presentation, with a hemoglobin A1cof 13%. Optical coherence tomography scans from the same day showed retinal edema with intraretinal fluid accumulation in both eyes (central subfield thickness: 320 nm OD, 764 nm OS) with foveal detachment in the left eye. She was diagnosed with severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy with macular edema in both eyes. She received 2 and 3 injections of bevacizumab in the right and left eyes, respectively, followed by 2 injections of aflibercept in both eyes with minimal effect on the edema. * DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Immunoglobulin (Ig) A multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy A. Order serum protein electrophoresis The lack of substantial central macular leakage on fluorescein angiography suggests that abnormal vascular permeability was not the major mechanism for the edema, and thus, injection of additional or alternative anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (C) or intravitreal corticosteroids (B) would likely not have helped. Although semaglutide (D) has been associated with worsening diabetic retinopathy, the patient had macular edema shortly after starting semaglutide, making it unlikely to be the cause of the macular edema. Additionally, worsening diabetic retinopathy associated with glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists is not commonly associated with worsening macular edema. Although the shape of the foveal detachment in the left eye is unusual for diabetic macular edema, this alone would not warrant workup for a nondiabetic cause of the retinal findings. However, in conjunction with the lack of response to anti-VEGF injections and atypical fluorescein angiography findings, further workup for a nondiabetic cause of the findings is indicated. Baseline laboratory work revealed anemia, elevated white blood cell count, and elevated serum creatinine, raising suspicion for a hyperviscosity syndrome. Thus, serum protein electrophoresis (A) was recommended as the next step in the workup. This step revealed an M-spike, which prompted quantitative immunoglobin analysis that revealed an elevated IgA result (2441 mg/dL). Bone marrow biopsy revealed 40% to 50% plasma cell infiltration, confirming the diagnosis of IgA multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy. Paraproteinemia describes the presence of excessive monoclonal globulins in the blood, typically due to underlying immunoproliferative disorders such as Waldenström macroglobulinemia or multiple myeloma.1Excessive paraprotein in the blood leads to hyperviscosity, which can manifest as venous stasis retinopathy, retinal hemorrhages, and optic disc edema. An infrequent issue in paraproteinemic maculopathy is the presence of serous macular detachment.1-5It is proposed that hyperviscosity causes venous stasis and hypoxia of the endothelial cells, weakening the blood-retinal barrier, leading to accumulation of immunoglobulins in the subretinal space. The consequent osmotic gradient created by the immunoglobulins leads to serous macular detachments.1,5-7Additionally, risk factors like anemia and diabetes can exacerbate the process by inducing hypoxia and further damaging the blood-retinal barrier, leading to increased leakage of immunoglobulins.1 Primary treatment is directed at decreasing blood paraprotein levels through systemic treatments.8In a case series of 33 patients with paraproteinemic maculopathy, there was no definitive improvement with intravitreal anti-VEGF or corticosteroid agents. The long-term visual prognosis is guarded, with approximately 40% of cases having unchanged or worsening maculopathy despite adequate treatment of paraproteinemia.1 Patients with type 2 diabetes frequently have subclinical diabetes years before being diagnosed. Patients can present with advanced retinopathy shortly after diagnosis, thus making it an important differential to consider. However, this case underscores the importance of considering hyperviscosity syndromes for patients with diabetes and atypical macular edema unresponsive to anti-VEGF treatment. Early diagnosis is crucial because ocular symptoms may be the first indicators of paraproteinemia. The patient was referred to an oncologist and began chemotherapy. Twelve weeks later, her visual acuity improved to 20/40 OD and 20/80 OS. On optical coherence tomography, the central subfield thicknesses changed to 435 nm OD and 406 nm OS. Her IgA level improved to 106 mg/dL.

A 52-year-old woman presented with decreased vision in both eyes. She was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 3 months before presentation, with a hemoglobin A1cof 13%. At that time, she was given metformin and semaglutide for glucose control. Her visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/200 OS. Fundus examination revealed retinal hemorrhages, hard exudates, and microaneurysms bilaterally (Figure, A and B). Fluorescein angiography revealed microaneurysms with noncentral leakage in the posterior pole with absence of significant ischemia and capillary dropout. Optical coherence tomography scans from the same day showed retinal edema with intraretinal fluid accumulation in both eyes (central subfield thickness: 320 nm OD, 764 nm OS) with foveal detachment in the left eye. She was diagnosed with severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy with macular edema in both eyes. She received 2 and 3 injections of bevacizumab in the right and left eyes, respectively, followed by 2 injections of aflibercept in both eyes with minimal effect on the edema. Blood analysis showed the following values: hemoglobin, 10.4 g/dL; red blood cell count, 3.30 × 106/μL; white blood cell count, 10 470/μL; platelets, 197 × 103/μL; fasting blood glucose, 150 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0555); normal lipid profile; and creatinine, 1.2 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4). Hemoglobin A1cdecreased to 6.8% at 7 months after presentation.

case_info.scenario: A 52-year-old woman presented with decreased vision in both eyes. She was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 3 months before presentation, with a hemoglobin A1cof 13%. At that time, she was given metformin and semaglutide for glucose control. Her visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/200 OS. Fundus examination revealed retinal hemorrhages, hard exudates, and microaneurysms bilaterally (Figure, A and B). Fluorescein angiography revealed microaneurysms with noncentral leakage in the posterior pole with absence of significant ischemia and capillary dropout. Optical coherence tomography scans from the same day showed retinal edema with intraretinal fluid accumulation in both eyes (central subfield thickness: 320 nm OD, 764 nm OS) with foveal detachment in the left eye. She was diagnosed with severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy with macular edema in both eyes. She received 2 and 3 injections of bevacizumab in the right and left eyes, respectively, followed by 2 injections of aflibercept in both eyes with minimal effect on the edema. Blood analysis showed the following values: hemoglobin, 10.4 g/dL; red blood cell count, 3.30 × 106/μL; white blood cell count, 10 470/μL; platelets, 197 × 103/μL; fasting blood glucose, 150 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0555); normal lipid profile; and creatinine, 1.2 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4). Hemoglobin A1cdecreased to 6.8% at 7 months after presentation.
case_info.caption: Widefield late-phase fluorescence angiography images of the right (A) and left (B) eye demonstrating areas of microaneurysms with mild leakage and absence of serious ischemia or capillary dropout. The top left insert in each panel shows the pseudocolor widefield fundus photographs demonstrating retinal hemorrhages, hard exudates, and microaneurysms in the right and left eye. The bottom inserts of each panel show macular optical coherence tomography imaging at presentation (bottom left) and after the patient received intravitreal injections (bottom right) over 6 months. The right eye demonstrates refractory retinal edema. The left eye demonstrates refractory retinal edema with neuroretinal detachment. The white asterisks indicate intraretinal edema; the yellow asterisks indicates neuroretinal detachment.
case_info.explanation: Immunoglobulin (Ig) A multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy A. Order serum protein electrophoresis The lack of substantial central macular leakage on fluorescein angiography suggests that abnormal vascular permeability was not the major mechanism for the edema, and thus, injection of additional or alternative anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents (C) or intravitreal corticosteroids (B) would likely not have helped. Although semaglutide (D) has been associated with worsening diabetic retinopathy, the patient had macular edema shortly after starting semaglutide, making it unlikely to be the cause of the macular edema. Additionally, worsening diabetic retinopathy associated with glucagon-like peptide 1 agonists is not commonly associated with worsening macular edema. Although the shape of the foveal detachment in the left eye is unusual for diabetic macular edema, this alone would not warrant workup for a nondiabetic cause of the retinal findings. However, in conjunction with the lack of response to anti-VEGF injections and atypical fluorescein angiography findings, further workup for a nondiabetic cause of the findings is indicated. Baseline laboratory work revealed anemia, elevated white blood cell count, and elevated serum creatinine, raising suspicion for a hyperviscosity syndrome. Thus, serum protein electrophoresis (A) was recommended as the next step in the workup. This step revealed an M-spike, which prompted quantitative immunoglobin analysis that revealed an elevated IgA result (2441 mg/dL). Bone marrow biopsy revealed 40% to 50% plasma cell infiltration, confirming the diagnosis of IgA multiple myeloma with paraproteinemic maculopathy. Paraproteinemia describes the presence of excessive monoclonal globulins in the blood, typically due to underlying immunoproliferative disorders such as Waldenström macroglobulinemia or multiple myeloma.1Excessive paraprotein in the blood leads to hyperviscosity, which can manifest as venous stasis retinopathy, retinal hemorrhages, and optic disc edema. An infrequent issue in paraproteinemic maculopathy is the presence of serous macular detachment.1-5It is proposed that hyperviscosity causes venous stasis and hypoxia of the endothelial cells, weakening the blood-retinal barrier, leading to accumulation of immunoglobulins in the subretinal space. The consequent osmotic gradient created by the immunoglobulins leads to serous macular detachments.1,5-7Additionally, risk factors like anemia and diabetes can exacerbate the process by inducing hypoxia and further damaging the blood-retinal barrier, leading to increased leakage of immunoglobulins.1 Primary treatment is directed at decreasing blood paraprotein levels through systemic treatments.8In a case series of 33 patients with paraproteinemic maculopathy, there was no definitive improvement with intravitreal anti-VEGF or corticosteroid agents. The long-term visual prognosis is guarded, with approximately 40% of cases having unchanged or worsening maculopathy despite adequate treatment of paraproteinemia.1 Patients with type 2 diabetes frequently have subclinical diabetes years before being diagnosed. Patients can present with advanced retinopathy shortly after diagnosis, thus making it an important differential to consider. However, this case underscores the importance of considering hyperviscosity syndromes for patients with diabetes and atypical macular edema unresponsive to anti-VEGF treatment. Early diagnosis is crucial because ocular symptoms may be the first indicators of paraproteinemia. The patient was referred to an oncologist and began chemotherapy. Twelve weeks later, her visual acuity improved to 20/40 OD and 20/80 OS. On optical coherence tomography, the central subfield thicknesses changed to 435 nm OD and 406 nm OS. Her IgA level improved to 106 mg/dL.
